প্রচ্ছদপ্রকাশিত লেখালেখক
কথাসাহিত্য

The Pull of the Roots

Mostafa Auvi (মোস্তফা অভি) · 2026-10-28

I met Umme Kulsum thirty years ago. After many childless years, I heard one day that a woman of uncommon holiness lived in the middle of the city. She counseled people toward good works, and for the sick she recited the words of God and prayed their afflictions away. Through her intercession, people said, many women had already conceived. Within a few days I had tracked her down.

I still can’t say how devout or how pure Umme Kulsum truly was. From morning until dusk, the Lord’s name was present in everything she did. When she slept, anyone who looked at her lips might have thought she was reciting His name in her dreams. She was a hafiz, one who carries the entire Quran in memory. When she lifted the verses of God’s book in that thin, glossy voice, it seemed the harmony of it might leave the very air senseless. She hummed as she gave the children their lessons, and the children, soaked in her tenderness, recited the verses in one unbroken stream. I had no children, and I was a solitary person. My husband left every morning for work and I was left utterly alone. I didn’t even have a neighbor to whom I could unload what had gathered inside me. In that bleak and hollow season, I found Umme Kulsum, and she became my friend.

From the heart of the city, a narrow lane splits the belly of the main road and runs inward, lined on both sides with small houses under the trees. Past three or four of them there is a stretch of fallow ground, a bed of grass, and a little farther on an old pond choked with water hyacinth. On the bank of that pond stands a long two-story building, a madrasa where girls memorize the Quran, and Umme Kulsum was its principal, its mohtamim. Her face was fair and round. Her eyes were almond-shaped, her eyebrows soft and curved like the young leaves of a tree, and her hair was so thickly, gleamingly black that no one looking at her head could look away. After the dawn prayer, this volunteer of God would open the Quran and read a page or two. Her voice was as bewitching as a flute, and her Arabic flowed like an Arab’s. Her company and her blessings, her prayers and the soft blowing of verses over the body, made me begin to believe that a child might yet take root in my womb. The place was remote, and she and I slept in a wooden loft above the ground floor. After supper, before sleep, we talked about many things, even the private hours between my husband and me. I listened to everything she said like a dutiful audience, and I fell asleep listening. And almost every night I dreamed ugly dreams about her. If those dreams were gathered into one, they would say that behind the principal and the pious woman, Umme Kulsum was a liar, a fraud, an adulteress. But in the waking world I had never seen anything of the kind in her.

Every Thursday night, women in black burqas came to the madrasa from the surrounding neighborhoods. They sat cross-legged in a purified silence, turned toward their Creator, and Umme Kulsum sat at the center and spoke of the essence of Islam. When she began telling the radiant old stories of the faith, her voice thick with feeling, something inside my chest seemed to spill like water. I would look at the listeners and see tears running down the cheeks of those middle-aged women. They passed through the invisible curtain of this world and were lost in another. I felt a deep respect for Umme Kulsum’s love of her faith, for the sheer ardor of it.

One day a woman in the neighborhood died, and Umme Kulsum was sent for to prepare the body for burial. Along the road that cuts the city from west to east, she was a name that many people knew. Whenever a Muslim woman died, she was called. She knew how to wash the dead properly and wrap them in the shroud. That day I had the good fortune of watching, from very close, everything that goes into making a body ready for the grave. When Umme Kulsum prepared the woman for washing, she never once looked at the dead woman’s unclothed body. She stood a little way off and worked the rites of purification with both hands moving in perfect rhythm. Then she steeped jujube leaves in warm water, and with that water began pouring over the whole body. When it was finished she dressed the dead woman beautifully, checked the cotton in the nose and ears, gathered the shroud at the head and the feet into two small knots, like a wrapped parcel, and began to pray over her: From it We created you, and into it We shall return you, and from it We shall bring you forth once again.

The women of the household praised her work. The dead woman’s relatives paid Umme Kulsum an advance for reciting the whole Quran in the deceased’s name, honoring her sacred labor. In a word, there was not another woman as righteous as this one in all that corner of the city. Little by little, I became a devotee of her single-minded striving for God’s pleasure. I joined her at every prayer. When she recited, I took the words into my heart like honey. I drew her water for ablutions, I prepared her meals, and it satisfied me down to my bones. For me Umme Kulsum became that radiant woman of Islam’s history, a second Rabia of Basra.

One day, toward dawn, I woke suddenly. I turned over and she was not beside me. She was crouched at a tin trunk, her hand inside it, switching on a light, looking at something. After the call to prayer she placed whatever it was back in the trunk with great care, performed her ablutions, and stood to pray. Listening to the Quran pour out of her in the last hours of the night, I was so enchanted that I wanted to stay near this holy woman for the rest of my life.

On another night I saw her at the trunk a second time. As a yaksha watches over treasure buried in the earth, Umme Kulsum guarded her object, bent over it, rapt. After that, every time I woke in the night I lay waiting for the moment when she would take some priceless thing from the trunk and gaze at it. Some nights the chance really did come to me. Other nights I slept like the senseless and dawn arrived and carried the hour I had waited for away.

After a few nights, her secret looking had become a curiosity that ate at me. The fourth time I saw her bent over the trunk in the same way, I rose from the bed with great caution. I lifted my heels and followed her on the balls of my feet. What was this hidden thing that she gazed at so deeply at the end of every night? Whatever was invisible to me, whatever made me curious, I wanted to pull into the light. I crept up behind her and stood close to her back, a hunger in me that couldn’t be satisfied. I was desperate to see something precious, something that would matter to me. I bent my spine like a bow and looked toward her hands. And what I saw was truly astonishing. Before surrendering herself to God, this virtuous woman looked, each time, at a few old and ruined photographs. I can’t say which god of the Sanatan faith they showed, but I’m sure they were pictures of some supreme deity. Every day, Umme Kulsum sat in a trance, gazing at that photograph. I turned and left without a sound. My body trembled in small waves. In an instant, something had struck my faith somewhere, and for a long time I couldn’t climb out of my bewilderment. I didn’t ask Umme Kulsum anything. I lay down and said nothing.

Three or four days passed in a sorrowful silence. The woman who, once she started talking, could not be stopped, had gone completely quiet. Umme Kulsum sank so deep into her thoughts that she forgot to eat. While teaching the children she stumbled over the pronunciation of the verses. In a few days such sadness settled on her face that it seemed I was looking at a thin person from a war-torn country. Finally, one day, I worked up the courage and asked her about the wooden box inside her trunk. And Umme Kulsum began to tell me about the unbearable days of her childhood.

In short, it happened like this. When I was thirteen, we lived in a remote village not far from the Bongaon station, in India. There were four of us: my father, Ajoy Pal, and my mother, Indubala. I was Krishnarani Pal, and I had a little brother whom I lovingly called Dada, big brother, though he was the younger. We were always together. I loved my brother so much that I never let him out of my sight. I thought I would pass eternity like this, with Dada, and that these sweet hours could never come to an end.

I was too young to understand the country, or the times, or what was unfolding around us. We lived as a child’s mind lives, dreaming and playing the hours away. We didn’t know the walls of caste and creed, or the gap between Hindu and Muslim. We played with Muslim boys and girls in the same neighborhood, in and out of each other’s yards. At the time of the Pujas we were happiest of all, going to our neighbors’ houses to eat the prasad, buying small treasures at the fair. And when the priest read the verses of the Gita over the loudspeaker, I would stand with my hand on a post in some corner and stare at his face in wonder. That joy of childhood will never come back. Because religion had never been a fence around us, we lived so freely that it never occurred to us that one day those happy times would turn into the distant past.

Then, one day, everything that had seemed normal changed. Our house wasn’t far from the village market. One afternoon, from the bridge by the bazaar, came the sound of a crowd of men shouting. At times it rolled through the air like thunder: Allahu Akbar. When the sound came in bursts, it seemed the earth would crack open and every house would be swallowed into an abyss. As the shouting came closer, then fell into silence, a different voice thickened the air from the east. Many raised throats cried out, Bande Mataram. And from another side, in time with the footfalls of hundreds of men, I heard Jai Shri Ram.

In an instant the whole village was in uproar. A war of blood broke out between Hindus and Muslims. I was so small then, and my heart was thrown into such wild disorder. The house next to ours burned, the flames roaring, and the bodies began to fall one by one. It was unimaginable. The neighbors in whose courtyards we had played were our nearest kin, and now, suddenly, they were our enemies. What happened to the women in every house is beyond description. The men were killed, the women dragged by their hair into the open and violated. Muslims burned Hindu houses and Hindus drove Muslims from their land. The riots stretched longer and longer until at last they grew long-lived. Every day, in Hindu or Muslim quarters, someone was murdered. Like smoke, an unbearable restlessness spread in every direction. We were cornered, helpless, in our own land.

One day the shadow of the riot reached our house too. At noon, I was lying on a quilt on the floor, asleep like the dead, when the sound of many feet and many raised voices outside tore me awake. As I sat up, a band of Muslims, shouting Allahu Akbar, threw themselves at our house before my eyes. A group of armed men dragged my father, Ajoy Pal, out of the house. I never saw when my mother vanished with my little brother. From all sides came the weeping of neighbors, but I had no time to look. To save my life I hid in a corner. And they killed my father, Ajoy Pal, right in front of me. By the time the Muslims left the house, evening had come and gone. For a long while I didn’t come out. I stayed hidden and stared at my father’s still body lying face-up in the yard. As the night deepened, three neighbors who had survived by luck came and sat beside his body, murmuring to each other. I came out of my hiding place and stood before those familiar faces and burst into helpless crying. Before the night was over, the neighbors, the men I called Kaku, uncle, laid his body near our burned house and made arrangements to cremate him. I couldn’t bear to watch my father’s body burn, so I walked out and sat quietly a little way off. Following the custom of our faith, the neighbors gathered his ashes into a clay pot and put it into my hands. Then they said goodbye and left. By then, the light of dawn had started up in the east.

In daylight I searched everywhere for my mother and found her nowhere. The burned house stood silent, like a lonely person. I didn’t know where to go by myself. I had two precious things in my hands then. One was a small wooden box. Inside it was a beautiful photograph of Lord Krishna. In the face of that infant lord of Gokul I saw the smile of heaven and I would lose myself in it. I loved that picture so much that I kept it in a little wooden box, always within reach. In the same box I had also kept a photograph from my parents’ wedding, a sweet memory of their time together. After searching all day for my mother, I went toward evening to my aunt’s house. I found no one there either. Then I went to my grandmother’s house, and when I stood in the yard, my whole body went cold. The entire house was as still as a cremation ground. There wasn’t a sound anywhere. I took the clay pot and the wooden box and went back to our own homestead. By then the whole village was a cremation ground. There wasn’t a human soul in sight. Everyone had run from the village in whatever way they could, toward an unknown somewhere. With my father’s ashes and my dear wooden box I waited three or four days on our land. One afternoon I heard that the fire of the riots had spread from the city to the villages, everywhere. In the last two days, hundreds of Muslims had been killed, and the survivors were leaving through the western border toward Pakistan. That evening I saw crowds of men, women, and children, walking from far and near toward the eastern border. Without a thought, I climbed down into the marsh and followed that crowd until I reached the border. No one stopped me. Together with hundreds of Muslims I crossed through the Jessore region into Bangladesh.

When I crossed over, afternoon had slipped into dusk. My senses had stopped working. I felt like a drowning person. That I was still alive in the world was itself a wonder to me. I couldn’t think where on this side I could find a safe place to rest. In that daze I kept walking, guarding the wooden box like a beloved object and my father’s ashes with it, like a woman gone astray. A little while later a thick darkness fell over the land. Slowly the people who had walked with me split off onto different roads and thinned out. I walked on in fear until I came to the front of a marketplace. A few people were still buying and selling. Two or three shops were open. I dropped onto a stool in front of an abandoned shop. Sleep came over both my eyes all at once. I slept in a filthy, run-down place where dogs wandered. Toward dawn I woke and found my wooden box in the hands of an old woman who stood over me. Her face was folded with wrinkles, the cloth of her head drawn low over her forehead. I greeted her with a namaskar, my palms together. She knotted her brows and stared at me and said, “Konthe jabu, bachha?” Where will you go, child?

I told her everything that had happened to me, from beginning to end. She thought for a while, then told me to follow her. With the wooden box and my father’s ashes, I walked behind the old woman. She lived at the far end of a poor village in a poor house. The road was long, a dirt path through the village, and along it lay the droppings of cattle. The old woman pointed at the cows and said the Hindus had left them behind and gone across the border, and now the Muslims were their guardians. She had no children, and her husband had died many years before. She had no household to speak of. She lived out her days in a tiny hut. I took shelter in her house. She was a Muslim, with an unshakable faith in God, and to her anyone of another religion was an infidel. At first, she called me Nomor chhuri, a low-caste Hindu girl. The word Nomo was bound up with the smile on her wrinkled cheeks, and I didn’t think much of it then. Because I was a Hindu girl, she wanted to purify me and bring me into the house. And for the purification she arranged a bath, which was truly strange and frightening. First she filled an earthen jar with the tidal water of the river and set it in a corner of the yard. Then she sat me on a wooden stool and took off my clothes. I should have felt shame, but there was no room for any. And yet the hair around my private parts had only just begun to grow, and the nipples of my breasts had only just come up. When I tried to stop her from baring me, the old woman flared up. With one hard jerk, she pulled the rest away.

First she laid a handful of young mango leaves on my head and muttered over them for a while. Then she shaved the hair from my head with a razor, and the three or four hairs under my arms as well. She laid me on a long wooden plank, smeared my whole body with clay, and cleared away the hair that had begun to grow like petals. When the bath was done, she dried me gently and dressed me in a seamless cloth of unbleached cotton. It was truly an inconceivable experience. I had never faced a moment for which I was so unprepared.

After I was bathed and purified in this way, she spread out a mat and made me sit facing the qibla, the direction of Mecca. She placed my right hand on the palm of her left and began the lesson of becoming a Muslim. In a slurred voice, she said: La ilaha illallah, Muhammadur Rasulullah. I watched the movement of her mouth and repeated her words in a low voice. I didn’t know what else I would have to endure in order to fall away from my faith. But I grew more determined, and in my heart I begged the Lord for help. Because at that moment, none of what was being done to me was something I was ready for. But the old woman was single-souled in matters of faith, and she called a muezzin from the mosque to finish the work of initiating me into my new religion. She laughed, she told stories of the old days, and yet she was a pitiless and cruel woman. To bear the situation I held as much patience as I could, and I walked on to keep the road ahead unbroken. Thanks to the muezzin, the news spread through the whole area: A cursed girl from a Nomo house has begun to live with the old woman.

From every side, the scorn and curses of contempt rained down on us. One night, holding the old woman’s hand, I left that border village and set out on a long road. After dusk we walked along the left side of a great highway. We met very few people on the way. Then came empty paths, marshes, a bridge made of bamboo, and a vast embankment. On the roadside were flowering trees of every kind, and near them stood the houses of Hindus, which the Muslims had probably wiped out. At the edge of the road a few dogs sat, as if in council. Mute creatures, they sat there panting, perhaps remembering the masters who had left the country. By dawn we reached a railway station.

By the time we reached this old town of one lane, the middle of the day had passed. In the sky a low drumming of clouds. As soon as we arrived at our destination, the storm and rain began. The house where we took shelter was the old woman’s father’s house. In this new family I came face to face with a new life. The old woman’s brother was an elder, and his sons were scholars of religion. They wore their hair in long locks, and each had a beard that reached down to his knees. Their mustaches were shaved, and their eyelashes were dark with kohl. All around the house, cut banana leaves had been fastened up as a screen, so that the place was hidden from view. The women inside were thin as sticks. They covered their bodies, and before every task they praised God. The house was old, and there was no lack of food. In front of the house, beside the narrow canal, was a row of boats belonging to the traders. Close by was a madrasa of long standing. What the old woman said to her brother and her nephews, I don’t know, but from the next day a new chapter began in my life. I became a student in the Nurani Qaida class, learning the alphabet of the Quran. From Krishnarani, I became Umme Kulsum.

Every night in the last hours before dawn, my lessons began with a veteran woman hafiz. When the call to prayer rose, I stood for the prayer. At each prayer I read one verse of the Quran and ended. Because at that time I knew no other chapter, no other word of God. When I passed the first stage of hifz, the memorization, the women who ran the madrasa burst with delight in my praise. Their bubbling admiration made me more determined. But I still had not given my father’s ashes any peace. By the time I had memorized fifteen paras, fifteen of the thirty parts of the Quran, my memory was so clear and sharp that the teachers boasted of me, saying: This girl who came from far away has astonished us. None of that praise moved me. In my mind I made a plan for my father’s ashes. I was a person from another country, another people. It was impossible for me to go anywhere far. But in my heart I vowed that by whatever means, I must give my father’s ashes their full dignity.

One day, at the hour of the true dawn, the principal woke me from sleep. I finished my purification and sat down to recite. Suddenly, from somewhere inside me, I heard my father Ajoy Pal’s soul call me again and again. It seemed to me that from the world of the gods, my father’s disembodied spirit was begging me for release. Before the light of morning came, I left the madrasa.

I followed the bank of the rushing canal upstream. Far from the river’s edge, there were houses, one here, another there. Because the weather was against us, I saw no herds of cattle, no gangs of herdboys, not even a farmer on his way to the field. I put the clay pot into a cloth bundle. Because it might rain, I covered it with a sheet of polythene and walked straight east. After a time I reached a lonely place where small trees and wild vines had braided together and made the ground dark. I judged it the right place and went slowly toward the current of the canal. First I opened the bundle and took the clay pot out. I untied the knotted cloth from around its neck and laid the white ashes in my palm. Then, with great care, I gave them to the water. In that still and unshaking dawn, not one speck of ash flew away on the wind. The few that clung to my palm I licked clean and swallowed. Then I sprinkled the canal water over my head, sank the clay pot beneath the surface, and climbed up the bank. There was one more precious thing I owned. If I had buried it in that lonely place, I could never have seen my father’s memory again. So I went back to the madrasa, dug a small hole in a corner of its yard, and buried what remained of my father there. It was an agony for me, but even so, after much searching I found and planted a tulsi bush in that spot. Now there is not so much as a trace of that plant.

When I was fifteen, my hair grew long and fell below my waist. The women of the madrasa were so overcome by my beauty that when their eyes fell on my face, they would say in a pure, hushed voice: Subhanallah. By then I had finished hifz and enrolled in the next course. The old woman who had sheltered me left me an orphan again and died. It was as if I had fallen into a shoreless sea. The family that had taken me in began preparing to marry me off. But the truth the old woman spoke about me on her deathbed shattered everything in an instant. The family rescued itself from the burden by making me a principal at this madrasa. And I was left counting the hours of an uncertain future.

I believe in the One who sees the truth, and I remember my mother and father. Every night in the last hours before dawn, when I wake, I open the wooden box and look at the beloved photographs of my childhood and remember. Each day, inside the photograph of Lord Krishna, I see my childhood. Then I worship God, and with my heart at peace I lose myself in humming my recitation. At the end of every day I say this truth aloud: in the Creator’s world, I am nothing but a human being. And even if it is the day before my death, I want to go back to the place where I was born.
